purpose: The way around a product — a nav landmark holding a list of destinations, one of which may be the page the user is on. It replaces the pipe-separated row of links v0 copy-pasted into five screens, which has no landmark, no current-page marker, and a separator that is a text character.
responsibilities: Render a real <nav> landmark with an accessible name, so it can be jumped to and skipped past.
Hold the destinations in a real list, so they are counted.
Mark at most one destination as the current page, with aria-current="page".
Draw a separator as a box decoration rather than as content.
Nothing about routing. It renders anchors and has no opinion about what happens when one is followed.
Nothing about which destination is current. The screen knows; this component is told.
do: Name it for what it is FOR — Main, Account, Footer — and leave the word navigation out, because the role already says it.
Mark the current page. It is the only thing that answers "where am I" for somebody who cannot see which label is heavier.
Keep the current destination a link. It is still somewhere a user can go, and removing it changes how many tab stops the bar has depending on which page you are on.
Let the labels wrap. Arabic runs to 117 per cent of English on some strings, and a bar that refuses to wrap clips a destination instead.
dont: Do not put the word "navigation" in the label. aria-label="Main navigation" is announced as "Main navigation navigation".

Do not use a text character as a separator. v0 uses a literal pipe, which is content — so it is announced — and is a Unicode-neutral character, so it reorders with its surroundings in Arabic instead of staying between two things.
Do not mark more than one destination current. aria-current="page" answers a question that has one answer.
Do not set aria-current="false" on the others. That is a stated claim repeated on every destination, and absence says the same thing more quietly.
Do not use a button for a destination. A control that changes the address is a link wearing the wrong element, and it loses the middle-click, the copy-link and the open-in-new-tab that came free.
Do not signal the current page with colour alone. The hover state uses the same two neutral tokens, so colour alone would make "where I am" and "where my pointer is" the same appearance.

do_not_use_when.when: The links are inside a sentence or a paragraph of prose.
do_not_use_when.use_instead: A plain <a>. A landmark around an inline link tells a screen-reader user there is a navigation region where there is only a sentence.

do_not_use_when.when: The items perform actions on the current screen rather than going somewhere.
do_not_use_when.use_instead: Button. If it does not change the address it is not a destination, and a toolbar of actions is not a navigation landmark.

do_not_use_when.when: Exactly one item is chosen and the choice is the point — a filter set, a segmented control.
do_not_use_when.use_instead: RideCard, whose RideCardGroup is a real radio group. Choosing is not navigating.

do_not_use_when.when: The destinations are a plain collection to read rather than the way around the product — related products, recent orders.
do_not_use_when.use_instead: List. It gives the counted-list semantics without claiming a landmark, and a page with five navigation landmarks has none.

do_not_use_when.when: The navigation is a hierarchy with expandable sections, or a breadcrumb trail.
do_not_use_when.use_instead: Nothing yet. Both are real components with their own semantics — a tree needs expanded state, a breadcrumb needs an ordered list and a separator rule of its own — and neither is built.

alternatives.for: a collection of links that is not the way around the product
an item that acts on this screen rather than going somewhere
a set where exactly one is chosen — its RideCardGroup is the radio group

content: The destination labels, which name where they go.
The landmark's name, which says which navigation this is.
constraints: No routing. This renders anchors; what a click does belongs to whatever router the application has.

No orientation prop. Both products' navigation is a horizontal row, and a vertical arrangement would change which axis the separator and the current marker sit on — a decision worth making with a real sidebar in front of it rather than in advance.
No dropdown, no submenu, no expandable section. A hierarchy needs expanded state this component does not have.
No skip link. It belongs to the page rather than to one landmark, and a component that emitted one would emit several on a page with several navigations.

No written numbers. The 1px separator and current-page rule were the seventh and last occurrence of the literal, and the count is what bought the scale: decision 026 added stroke.100 and stroke.200, and both resolve from stroke.100.
One value the token layer owes a name to: the 0.25em underline offset, which is the Arabic rule from §2 and the second place in the library to write it after ProductCard.

behaviour: This is the component where the inline axis actually matters. The row is laid out along the reading direction, the separator sits between items on that axis, and the current-page rule is drawn under them — three places a physical left or right would produce the half-flipped bar §1 says reads worse than one that did not flip at all.
The row is flex, so it reverses with the document and no rule names a side.

The separator is a border-inline-start on every item after the first. Verified in a browser rather than assumed: in an RTL page it resolves to the RIGHT edge, 1px there and 0 on the left, and the first destination is the rightmost.
The current-page rule is a border-block-end, so it stays underneath in both directions. It is deliberately not an inline-start marker, which would sit above the item in a vertical arrangement.

The hover underline declares text-underline-offset, because §2 records that Arabic carries dots below the baseline and a default underline is drawn straight through them. skip-ink is left at its initial auto and is not relied on: on an Arabic string it fires several times per word and delivers the link as four or five dashes.

letter-spacing 0 is declared rather than inherited. A navigation is short text, which is exactly where a page's global tracking is most often applied for effect, and tracking breaks the joins in Arabic script.
mirrors: The whole row, with the document.
The separator, which moves to the other side of each item.
does_not_mirror: The current-page rule, which is on the block axis and stays under the label in both directions.

guarantees: A real <nav> landmark, which v0 has nowhere in the application — so for the first time the navigation can be jumped to and skipped past.
An accessible name on every landmark, because label is required and a page may hold more than one.
The destinations in a real list with role="list" written explicitly, so they are counted after list-style: none removes the markers.
aria-current="page" on the current destination — the token rather than the generic true — and the attribute absent rather than false on the others.
The current page carried by three signals: the attribute, a weight and colour change, and a rule beneath it. Never colour alone, which would also be indistinguishable from hover.
Real anchors, so middle-click, copy-link, open-in-new-tab and the status-bar preview all work.
0 axe violations across all six stories, checked in dark + RTL.
consumer_must: Tell it which destination is current. This component cannot know the route, and a navigation with nothing marked is the v0 behaviour it exists to replace.
Mark at most one. Nothing here prevents two, and two answers to "where am I" is worse than none.
Provide the skip link. It belongs to the page, and a component that emitted one would emit several on a page with several navigations.
Keep the label free of the word navigation, and distinct from any other navigation landmark on the page.

use_when: A set of links is the way around the product.
One destination is the page the user is currently on and should be marked as such.
A screen-reader user should be able to jump to the navigation or skip past it.
not_a: A toolbar of actions. If an item does not change the address it is a Button, not a destination.
A radio group or a filter set. Choosing is not navigating.
A plain list of links. A collection to read is a List; a landmark is for the way around.
A breadcrumb or a tree. Both have semantics this does not have.
A router. It renders anchors and has no opinion about what following one does.

deprecation.policy: The last component of Stage 4 and the one most likely to grow rather than be withdrawn: a real product eventually wants a vertical arrangement, a submenu or a breadcrumb, and each of those is a decision about whether this component gains a mode or a sibling is built. The rule from decision 020 applies either way — one axis, one prop, and a new case is a new member of a union rather than a second prop beside it. A prop is withdrawn ahead of the component: @deprecated in the source with the replacement named in the tag, one minor version of overlap, then removal in a major one with the migration written down.

unmapped.why: The destinations are instances a designer places directly. There is no property to mirror.
It becomes aria-label — a name for assistive technology with no visual form. A Figma variant for it would be two identical frames.

label.guidance: Required, and it becomes aria-label on the landmark. Name it for what it is FOR — Main, Account, Footer — and leave the word navigation out: the role already says it, so "Main navigation" is announced as "Main navigation navigation". A page with two unnamed navigation landmarks is a page where a screen-reader user hears "navigation, navigation" and has to guess.

children.guidance: The destinations, each a NavigationItem. NavigationItem exists so a call site cannot forget the <li> and cannot reach for a <button> — a control that changes the address is a link wearing the wrong element.

separators.guidance: A border-inline-start on every item after the first, replacing v0's literal pipe. The pipe is wrong on two counts and only one is visual: it is content, so it is announced; and it is a Unicode-neutral character, so it reorders with its surroundings in Arabic rather than staying between two things. A border is a box decoration on the inline axis — invisible to a screen reader, and it changes side with the document.
